prompt:
A 78-year-old man with new onset heart rate of 120 while at rest, asymptomatic. He drinks 1 glass of wine weekly. His EKG shows atrial flutter with 2:1 block. BP elevated 151/98. What are the next best steps?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Assess hemodynamic stability and evaluate for chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, acute heart failure, or neurologic deficits.
Obtain or review a 12-lead ECG with rhythm strip to confirm atrial flutter and the ventricular response.
Determine the duration of atrial flutter and whether the onset time is known.
Order a complete blood count.
Order a comprehensive metabolic panel to assess renal function, electrolytes, and hepatic function.
Measure serum magnesium.
Order TSH with reflex free T4 to evaluate for thyroid disease.
Obtain a transthoracic echocardiogram to assess ventricular function and structural heart disease.
Calculate the CHA2DS2-VASc score to guide stroke prevention.
Assess bleeding risk and modifiable bleeding factors using a tool such as HAS-BLED.
Start a low-dose AV-nodal blocker for rate control, such as metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily or diltiazem extended-release 120 mg daily.
Avoid diltiazem or verapamil when pre-excitation or decompensated systolic heart failure is present.
Start therapeutic oral anticoagulation, such as apixaban 5 mg twice daily with dose adjustment when indicated by age, weight, and renal function.
Counsel the patient regarding the stroke-prevention benefit and bleeding risks of anticoagulation.
Refer to cardiology or electrophysiology for consideration of cavotricuspid isthmus ablation and rhythm-control options.

For elective cardioversion when flutter duration is at least 48 hours or unknown, provide at least three weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation beforehand, or use TEE to exclude atrial thrombus with therapeutic anticoagulation established before cardioversion.
Arrange follow-up within 1 to 2 weeks to reassess ventricular rate, blood pressure, and medication tolerance.
Provide urgent return precautions for chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, neurologic deficits, worsening palpitations, or signs of bleeding.
Counsel the patient to avoid stimulants such as excessive caffeine and sympathomimetic decongestants.
Repeat blood pressure measurements and address persistent hypertension without rapid blood-pressure lowering.
Administer IV adenosine with the expectation that it will terminate atrial flutter.
Perform synchronized cardioversion in this stable patient without an appropriate anticoagulation or TEE-guided strategy.
Use aspirin monotherapy as the sole method of stroke prevention.
Use dual antiplatelet therapy in place of oral anticoagulation.
Start flecainide or propafenone before excluding structural heart disease and providing AV-nodal blockade.
Use digoxin as first-line monotherapy for initial rate control.
Withhold anticoagulation solely because the patient is asymptomatic, elderly, or drinks little alcohol.
Start sotalol or amiodarone solely for acute rate control without appropriate monitoring.
Start high-dose combined beta-blocker and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker therapy.
Administer short-acting or sublingual nifedipine to rapidly lower the blood pressure.
Reassure the patient and defer rate control, stroke-risk assessment, and diagnostic evaluation.
Refer directly for pacemaker implantation for uncomplicated atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.
Administer thrombolytic therapy in the absence of an acute thrombotic indication.
Perform urgent coronary angiography solely to evaluate the atrial flutter without evidence of acute coronary syndrome.
Perform an exercise stress test during inadequately controlled atrial flutter rather than first addressing the ventricular rate.
Refer for urgent AV-node ablation before an adequate trial of pharmacologic rate control.
Administer diltiazem or verapamil when ventricular pre-excitation is present.
Recommend complete alcohol abstinence as the primary treatment for atrial flutter in a patient drinking one glass of wine weekly.

If cardioversion or flutter ablation is performed, continue therapeutic anticoagulation for at least four weeks afterward and base subsequent continuation on thromboembolic risk rather than apparent rhythm success.
